map_chunks.summary_text: This chunk discusses the diagnostic utility of SARS-CoV-2 testing modalities for COVID-19, particularly in the context of pre-travel testing policy. Acute COVID-19 diagnosis relies on NAAT [S1|PMC9012948_main|6775]. A Chinese Embassy policy (from 8 November 2020) mandated a 'dual test' (NAAT + IgM serology) within 48 hours of travel from Australia to China [S2|PMC9012948_main|6775]. Two key limitations of IgM serology are highlighted: (1) IgM has low sensitivity for detecting PCR-negative but potentially infectious individuals [S3|PMC9012948_main|6775], and (2) IgM is frequently positive beyond the infectious period, rendering mandatory negative dual-test requirements unnecessary [S4|PMC9012948_main|6775].

Two commercial in-laboratory SARS-CoV-2 antibody assays were evaluated [S1|PMC9012948_main|6776]: (1) the Roche Elecsys Anti-SARS-CoV-2 assay (Roche Total), which targets nucleocapsid IgM/IgA/IgG, and (2) the Abbott Architect SARS-CoV-2 IgM assay (Abbott IgM), which targets spike antibody. In-house validation demonstrated high specificity for both assays — 99.5% for Roche Total and 98.9% for Abbott IgM — values comparable to manufacturer-stated specificities of 99.8% and 99.56%, respectively [S2|PMC9012948_main|6776]. However, in-house sensitivity at 8–14 days post symptom onset in confirmed COVID-19 cases was 67% for both assays, substantially lower than the manufacturer-stated sensitivity of 85% [S3|PMC9012948_main|6776].

map_chunks.summary_text: This concluding passage addresses the practical limitations of IgM-based SARS-CoV-2 serology in the travel context, particularly for travellers to China [S1|PMC9012948_main|6787]. The Roche Total nucleocapsid-based assay is proposed as a screening tool that may reduce false-positive IgM rates among recently vaccinated travellers, since it does not detect vaccine-induced spike IgM [S2–S3|PMC9012948_main|6787]. However, individuals previously infected with SARS-CoV-2 will have detectable nucleocapsid antibodies with this assay; in the described laboratory workflow, these are subsequently tested with a lateral-flow nucleocapsid-specific IgM assay, and a positive result is likely to cause significant travel delays [S3–S4|PMC9012948_main|6787]. The authors highlight that IgM testing pitfalls carry major practical implications, including inconvenience and cost from postponed travel and additional testing, a situation expected to persist [S5|PMC9012948_main|6787]. Ultimately, NAAT alone is advocated as the most reliable indicator of infection risk in travellers, with the "dual-test" (IgM + NAAT) requirement considered problematic [S6|PMC9012948_main|6787].

findings.claim: Severe hypertriglyceridaemia (plasma TG >10 mmol/L) -> primarily polygenic etiology
findings.verbatim_support: Severe hypertriglyceridaemia, defined as plasma triglycerides > 10 mmol/L, is primarily polygenic and contributed by multiple acquired factors including diet, obesity, alcoholism, diabetes mellitus, hypothyroidism, paraproteinaemia and drugs. On the other hand, familial chylomicronaemia syndrome refers to a group of rare disorders of hypertriglyceridaemia, the most common being lipoprotein lipase deficiency (MIM #238600) due to pathogenic variants in the LPL gene (MIM *609708), with an estimated prevalence of 1 in 1,000,000. No known genotype-phenotype correlation exists in LPL deficiency [S1|PMC9012948_main|6803]. The LPL Ala98Thr variant decreases both secretion and catalytic activity of LPL, though with some residual activity preserved [S2|PMC9012948_main|6803], whereas the LPL Leu279Val variant almost completely abolishes catalytic activity [S3|PMC9012948_main|6803].
